analysis.one_liner: Extends federal gun-purchase background check waiting periods from three to ten business days.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Enhanced Background Checks Act 228-198 in February 2019, but the Senate never took a vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets a loophole in federal gun background checks. Today, if the FBI check is not finished within three business days, a licensed gun dealer can complete the sale anyway — this is how the Charleston church shooter in 2015 got his gun after his check stalled. The bill would raise that window to a minimum of ten business days, and would only let a sale proceed after that if the buyer filed a petition and another ten business days passed without the FBI resolving the check. It also directs federal agencies to study how the changes affect domestic violence victims, and replaces an outdated mental-health term in the law with clearer language.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially communities affected by gun violence. Closing or narrowing the three-day 'default proceed' window means records that surface late — a domestic violence conviction, a felony — can actually block a sale. The bill also directs the Justice Department to report on changes that would further protect victims of domestic violence, dating partner violence, sexual assault, and stalking, and requires public reporting on how many delayed checks the FBI never resolved.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum waiting period for a stalled background check from 3 business days to at least 10, so a delayed record has time to surface before a sale is completed.

Even after 10 days, a purchaser must submit a signed petition and wait another 10 business days before a dealer may transfer the firearm if the FBI still has not decided — making the expedited window roughly 20 business days, not 3.

Requires the GAO to report at 1, 3, and 5 years on whether the new procedures actually prevented gun transfers to people legally barred from buying them, and requires the FBI to publicly report how many petitions went unanswered within the deadline.

Directs the Attorney General, consulting a national resource center on domestic violence and firearms, to recommend further background check changes to reduce the risk of death or serious injury to victims of domestic and dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking.
Replaces the outdated statutory term 'adjudicated as a mental defective' with 'adjudicated with mental illness, severe developmental disability, or severe emotional instability.'

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers and prospective buyers. Dealers must hold pending sales longer — at least 10 business days, and roughly 20 when a buyer petitions — which slows sales and adds paperwork. Buyers whose checks are delayed, including people with common names or incomplete records who are legally allowed to own guns, wait weeks instead of days for the firearm they want.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the broader private-sale loophole untouched: unlicensed sellers, including many at gun shows and online, still do not have to run a background check at all, so some prohibited buyers can simply switch sellers.

Law-abiding buyers who get wrongly delayed — often because of a name or record mix-up — would wait at least 10 business days and, if they petition, around 20, a real burden for someone who needs a firearm for self-protection in the meantime.

The bill's protection depends entirely on FBI staffing: it lengthens the waiting window but does not fund the resources needed to resolve stalled checks faster, so the same delays that produced the problem could simply be shifted rather than fixed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a modest, targeted fix: keep a sale on hold longer when the government has not finished checking, so late-arriving disqualifying records can block it. The cost falls on a small group — buyers with delayed checks and dealers waiting on the FBI — and the bill builds in a petition path so no one is delayed forever. Its real limits are that it does nothing about sales between private individuals and does not fund faster FBI processing, so it narrows one well-known gap rather than closing the background check system's gaps generally.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 228-198, but the Senate never took it up; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended in January 2021, so the waiting-period change never became law.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee amended and approved the bill 21-14 on February 13, 2019, and reported it a week later.
On February 28, 2019, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit — which would have added an exception for domestic violence victims — 194 to 232, then passed the bill 228 to 198.
The vote was 225-7 among House Democrats and 3-191 among House Republicans, with 15 cosponsors including 1 Republican.
The Senate received the bill in early March 2019 and placed it on its calendar under General Orders, but no vote ever occurred; the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The three-business-day 'default proceed' window the bill targeted remains in federal law unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun dealers and the firearms advocacy groups that opposed extended waiting periods are better off, because the default-proceed window they defended stays exactly as it was. Buyers whose checks would have been delayed also keep the current three-day rule. Everyone affected by the loophole the bill targeted — including communities where stalled checks ended in shootings — got no change at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers and pro-gun advocacy groups

for.name: James E. Clyburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and moved it as House leadership priority shortly after Democrats took the House majority.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on February 13, 2019, approved the bill as amended 21-14, and reported it on February 22.

for.name: 14 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill 15 cosponsors including one Republican.

against.name: 191 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 191-3, and backed the failed motion to recommit that would have added a domestic violence victim exception.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote after it arrived on the Senate calendar in March 2019; it sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and lobbied against extended waiting periods; it rated the bill against members' voting records.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost cleanly by party: 225 of 231 voting Democrats yes and only 7 no; 191 of 197 voting Republicans no with only 3 yes. All 15 cosponsors but one were Democrats.

industries.note: The bill forces dealers to hold pending sales for at least 10 business days and roughly 20 when a buyer petitions, instead of the current 3, slowing turnover and adding compliance steps. Dealers' interest in the current short window runs against the safety benefit buyers and communities would get from letting checks finish.
Longer default-proceed delays can reduce some completed sales, which is why firearms advocacy groups opposed the bill. The same delay is what allows late-arriving disqualifying records to surface.
